# Handoff

Capture everything a fresh session needs to continue this work, so the current
session can be ended without losing ground.

**Why this exists.** Every turn re-reads the entire accumulated prefix, so cost
per turn climbs with session length — measured at ~26K cache-read tokens per
turn in short sessions versus ~109K past 100 turns. Ending a long session at a
clean boundary and restarting with a handoff is the largest available
efficiency lever. The handoff is what makes ending cheap.

## Where to write it

```
~/.claude/handoffs/<cwd-with-slashes-as-dashes>.md
```

For example, `/Users/rashford/Developer/kitsune` →
`~/.claude/handoffs/-Users-rashford-Developer-kitsune.md`

Overwrite any existing file for this directory — the newest handoff wins. The
`SessionStart` hook loads it automatically in the next session, so **do not**
paste the contents back into chat.

## What to write

Aim for something a competent stranger could act on. Be concrete: real paths,
real command names, real decisions. Skip anything reconstructible from the repo
or from `git log` — those are already available to the next session.

```markdown
# Handoff — <one-line description of the work>
Written: <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> · Session: <turns> turns

## Where things stand
Two or three sentences. What was being worked on and what state it is in
right now — not a history of the session.

## Decisions made (and why)
Only decisions that would otherwise be re-litigated. Include the reasoning,
because the reasoning is the part that gets lost.

## Files touched
- `path/to/file` — what changed and why

## What's verified vs assumed
Explicit. If tests ran, say so and give the result. If something was assumed
and never checked, say that too — this is the section that prevents the next
session from building on sand.

## Next step
The single next action, stated concretely. Then anything queued behind it.

## Open questions
Things the user needs to decide, or that were left unresolved.

## The confirmation handshake

Every mutating tool takes an optional `confirm` argument. Call it once **without**
`confirm` and nothing is sent to the controller — you get back a plan describing
the exact effect, the exact request body, and a token. Call it again with
identical arguments plus that token to execute.

The token is `sha256(operation | target | canonical_json(payload))[:12]`. Change
any argument that feeds the payload and the token stops matching, so a token
issued for one change cannot be replayed against a different one. This is a
**guard rail, not a security boundary** — a model could compute it in principle;
the point is that it cannot do so *accidentally*.

`target` is usually the bare object name, but it is not required to be. Where an
argument reaches the controller in the **URL path** rather than the body, it is
in neither the payload nor the object name, and folding it into `target` is the
only thing that binds the token to it. `nv_update_user_role` is the case that
matters: its `role` travels in the path, so its target is
`"<fullname> role=<role>"`, not `"<fullname>"`. Without that, a token previewed
for `role="reader"` would also authorise `role="admin"` — the handshake would
fail to gate the single field the tool exists to change. The controller call and
the request body are untouched by this; only the hashed target differs. Keep this
in mind when adding any mutating tool with path parameters.

### What `NV_ALLOWED_NAMESPACES` does not cover

`NV_ALLOWED_NAMESPACES` is deliberately absent from the five layers above. It is
a **narrowing hint, not a boundary**, and it is fail-open by construction: the
check runs only when the tool can name the namespace its change lands in.

Of the 67 mutating call paths, **18 name a namespace and are checked**; the
other 49 pass none and are unaffected by the setting. The uncovered set is not
an oversight — most of those writes have no namespace to name:

- **Genuinely cluster-wide objects.** Registries, sigstore roots and verifiers,
  webhooks, DLP and WAF *sensors*, system and scan config, admission rules,
  compliance profiles. These exist once per cluster.
- **All of `iam_write`.** Users, roles and API keys are cluster identities.
- **Writes addressed by opaque id.** A network rule id, a response rule id or a
  packet-capture id carries no namespace, and resolving one would cost a read
  per call that the guard deliberately does not make.

So `NV_ALLOWED_NAMESPACES=prod` stops a group, workload or service write landing
in `staging`. It does **not** stop `nv_delete_registry`, `nv_create_api_key` or
`nv_update_system_config`. Use `NV_TOOLSETS` to remove the toolsets a client has
no business calling, and provision the API key's NeuVector role to match — those
are the controls that hold.

Live verification of 1.1.1 against the 5.6.0 controller found the
stepping added in #44 was solving a problem that does not exist, and
that the read-back verifying it had a race that failed changes which
had in fact succeeded.

What #44 believed: the controller silently discards a mode move of more
than one rung, so Discover -> Protect must be walked through Monitor.

What is actually true: PATCH /v1/service/config is applied
asynchronously. It returns 200 before the change is readable, with a
measured lag of 0.33-0.59s over five runs. A GET issued immediately
after the 200 can still show the old value -- which is exactly what the
earlier session saw and read as "accepted and dropped".

Re-measured: five consecutive single-call Discover -> Protect moves all
landed, on both dimensions, including with the other dimension already
at Protect, and including the exact combination that failed during
verification. There is no adjacency rule.

So:

- plan_mode_patches() and mode_steps() are gone. One PATCH, the one the
  confirm token bound.
- verify_applied() replaces the single read-back with a bounded retry
  (8 x 0.5s) that returns on the first clean read. A change that lands
  late is not a change that failed; a change that never lands still
  raises UpstreamError naming the value the controller holds.
- FakeServices grew lag_reads=N, hiding a committed write from the next
  N reads. Every stepping test is replaced by one that asserts a single
  call, and both tools have a test that they survive the lag.

The two findings from #44 that were real are untouched and now
live-verified: profile_mode is a payload field (the /profile route is
inert), and the confirm token binds the dimension.

The read-back is what caught this. It was the part of #44 worth
keeping, and it earned its place by failing loudly on a change that had
succeeded rather than staying quiet.

Fix the High and Medium findings from the security/perf audit

Seven findings from an audit of the repo for security, performance and
correctness. Each was reproduced with an executed PoC before being
fixed, and each fix has a test that fails without it.

S2 (High) -- path traversal. All 63 tool endpoint paths are f-strings
interpolating a caller-supplied name. httpx resolves ".." against the
base URL, so an argument selected the endpoint: a read-only server with
only the compliance toolset reached GET /v1/user, and
nv_delete_group("../api_key/mcp-writer") issued DELETE
/v1/api_key/mcp-writer with the confirm handshake authorising it.
Fixed centrally with one validate_path() call at the top of
NeuVectorClient.request rather than by editing 63 f-strings -- a
central reject closes traversal and ?/# injection in one file with no
risk of a bad mechanical edit. "/" stays legal because a registry image
id genuinely is a repository path; going up still needs "..", which is
refused.

S1 (High) -- bearer scopes were decorative. nv:read/nv:write were
parsed, handed to StaticTokenVerifier and never read; an nv:read token
called nv_delete_group over real HTTP and the DELETE landed. Resolved
by removing the concept rather than enforcing it: privilege belongs to
the NeuVector API key's role, narrowed by NV_READ_ONLY, NV_TOOLSETS and
the confirm handshake. Two clients needing different power is two
Deployments. A legacy <token>:<scope> value is now a startup error, not
a silent strip -- stripping would preserve belief in a control that
never existed.

S9 (High) -- credential leak, found while fixing S1. Any Settings
validation failure rendered pydantic's input_value, i.e. the whole
settings dict, so a typo'd NV_TOOLSETS printed NV_API_SECRET_KEY and
NV_PASSWORD to stderr and on into the pod log. load_settings() now
re-raises ConfigError built from exc.errors(include_input=False) with
"from None" -- the from None matters, chaining reprints the leak.

P1 (High, correctness) -- writes were retried. client.request retried
every method 3x on a transient failure, including
ERR_FAIL_WRITE_CLUSTER and 502/504; a failing POST /v1/group was sent
three times. The retry budget is now GET-only, with a retry= kwarg for
a caller that knows its write is idempotent. login() is unaffected, it
bypasses request().

P2 (Medium) -- re-login stampede. The 401 handler took _login_lock and
called login() with no double-check, so ten concurrent 401s produced
ten POST /v1/auth and risked ERR_TOO_MANY_LOGIN_USER. Snapshot the
token before contending, re-check after acquiring. Measured 10 logins
before, 1 after.

S3 (Medium-High) -- NV_ALLOWED_NAMESPACES is fail-open, and was
overstated. nv_delete_group passed no namespace at all despite
_namespace_from_group_name existing three lines away; that is wired up,
taking coverage to 18 of 67 write paths. The other 49 were audited and
none can derive a namespace -- registries, webhooks and sigstore
objects are cluster-scoped, iam_write is cluster identities, and
network/response rules and packet captures are addressed by opaque id.
Making the guard fail closed would block those 49 rather than scope
them, so the fail-open is documented instead: in the authorise_write
docstring, in the config table, and in a new README section naming what
the setting does not cover.

S5 (Medium) -- NetworkPolicy ingress had no from: selector, so every
pod in the cluster could reach :8080 while the comment above it claimed
"Nothing else, in or out". Ingress is now opt-in via a
neuvector-mcp-client=true label. This does break the documented
off-cluster LoadBalancer path, which relied on the open rule, so the
README section that said the NetworkPolicy "needs no change" now says
the opposite and carries the ipBlock snippet.

Two deliberate non-changes:

- SPEC.md and neuvector-mcp-spec/ are untouched, though SPEC 7.2 now
  describes a retry policy the code no longer has and SPEC.md:260 still
  documents the old scope format. Editing the spec to match the code

- The three copies of _namespace_from_group_name stay three copies.
